summary: Defines a way for X.509 certificates to say that no revocation information is available. Short-lived certificates are not revoked because they expire faster than revocation could be distributed, and some long-lived ones are never revoked. It updates RFC 5280.

eli5.summary: Some certificates expire so fast that cancelling them is pointless. This lets a certificate say "don't look for a cancel list".

questions: how do short-lived certificates handle revocation
what does rfc 9608 change in rfc 5280
subtitle: A certificate extension that tells relying parties the CA publishes no revocation information, so they can skip revocation checks.

tldr.problem: Short-lived X.509 certificates expire faster than revocation could be detected, reported and distributed, and some long-lived certificates never expire or get revoked. Relying parties had no clear signal that no revocation information exists.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9608 profiles the noRevAvail extension (id-ce 56, a NULL value, non-critical) for end-entity certificates, and updates RFC 5280 path validation so the revocation check is skipped when it is present.
tldr.outcome: A CA can mark certificates it will never revoke. The cost is that revocation is bypassed entirely, so misuse could leave a relying party trusting a revoked certificate, and the only remedy is to revoke the CA.

today: RFC 9608 is a Proposed Standard from June 2024 that updates RFC 5280. It has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC.

sections.title: Why Some Certificates Have No Revocation
sections.content:
X.509v3 certificates with short validity periods are seeing greater use, for example through ACME (RFC 8555). A CA often publishes no revocation information for them, because the validity period is shorter than the time needed to detect, report and distribute revocation information. Revoking such a certificate, when it is used for authentication or key management, is described as unnecessary and pointless. Revoking a long-lived signature certificate, such as for document or code signing, still says something useful about when a compromise was discovered.

Some long-lived certificates never expire and are never revoked. The example given is an IDevID certificate installed in a device at the factory, binding the device identity to a key. To say a certificate has no well-defined expiry, the notAfter date is set to 99991231235959Z.

The new noRevAvail extension lets a relying party readily see that the CA does not publish revocation information. It is similar to the ocsp-nocheck extension of RFC 6960, but that one is meant only for certificates issued to OCSP responders, while noRevAvail suits any end-entity certificate. Implementers should not treat it as a substitute for ocsp-nocheck.
sections.eli5: If a ticket is only good for a few minutes, nobody bothers keeping a list of cancelled tickets. The note on the ticket says so.

sections.title: How the Extension Got Here
sections.content:
The history in the RFC runs as follows. In 1988 CCITT defined the X.509v1 certificate, and in 1997 ITU-T defined X.509v3 and the attribute certificate. In 1999 the IETF first profiled X.509v3 for the Internet (RFC 2459). In 2000 ITU-T defined noRevAvail for attribute certificates, and in 2002 the IETF profiled attribute certificates with support for it (RFC 3281).

ITU-T published an update to X.509 in 2019. Because short-lived certificates are used more widely, a recent Technical Corrigendum to X.509 allows noRevAvail to be used with public key certificates as well as attribute certificates.
sections.eli5: The note already existed for one kind of certificate. The rule makers recently let it be used on ordinary certificates too.

sections.title: The noRevAvail Extension
sections.content:
The extension, defined in the ITU-T corrigendum, lets a CA indicate that no revocation information will be made available for the certificate. Conforming CAs MUST include it in certificates for which no revocation information will be published, and MUST mark it non-critical. It MUST NOT be present in CA certificates.

Its name is id-ce-noRevAvail, its OID is { id-ce 56 }, and its syntax is NULL, which has the DER encoding 0500 in hex. The criticality MUST be FALSE.

A relying party that does not understand the extension might find a CRL from the CA, but the CRL will never include an entry for that certificate. Section 5 of the RFC gives an ASN.1 module for the extension.
sections.eli5: The note is tiny and says only 'nothing to see here'. Software that cannot read the note will still find no cancel list entry for the ticket.

sections.title: Rules for Other Extensions
sections.content:
Certificates that include noRevAvail MUST NOT include extensions that point to CRL repositories or give OCSP responder locations. If noRevAvail is present, then:

  • The certificate MUST NOT include basic constraints with the cA boolean set to TRUE.
  • It MUST NOT include the CRL Distribution Points extension.
  • It MUST NOT include the Freshest CRL extension.
  • Authority Information Access, if present, MUST NOT include an id-ad-ocsp access method.

If any of these rules is violated, the relying party MUST consider the certificate invalid.
sections.eli5: A ticket that says 'no cancel list' must not also point to a cancel list. If it does, the ticket is rejected.

sections.title: Change to Path Validation
sections.content:
Section 6.1.3 of RFC 5280 describes basic certificate processing in path validation. Step (a)(3) requires that, at the current time, the certificate is not revoked, determined using a CRL, status information or out-of-band means.

This RFC updates that step. If the noRevAvail extension is present, or the ocsp-nocheck extension is present, then step (a)(3) is skipped. Otherwise revocation status is determined as before.
sections.eli5: When the checker sees the note, it skips the step of looking up the cancel list. With no note, it checks as usual.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 5280 still apply. With noRevAvail in a certificate, all revocation checking is bypassed. CA policies and practices MUST ensure the extension is included only when appropriate, because misuse or misconfiguration could leave a relying party trusting a revoked certificate. The only possible remediation once misuse is found is revoking the CA.

Without revocation information, relying parties are less able to detect compromised keys, malicious certificates, or CAs that are not following their Certificate Policy or Certification Practices Statement. They therefore need confidence in the CA, and may evaluate its reliability, monitor its performance and observe its incident response.

For short-lived certificates, using the extension when the validity period is not adequately short gives attackers a window to exploit a compromised private key, so the period must be assessed carefully first. For long-lived certificates, such as IDevID certificates, the CA cannot notify relying parties of compromise of the factory-installed keys, so algorithms expected to stay secure for the device's lifetime need to be chosen.
sections.eli5: If the note is put on the wrong tickets, a stolen ticket keeps working. So the ticket office must be careful, and anyone checking tickets should trust the office.
